project.name: redis
project.description: Redis is an in-memory data structure store used as database, cache, and message broker. Single-threaded event loop, custom dynamic strings, custom hash tables with incremental rehashing, multiple persistence strategies (RDB snapshots, AOF append-only files), replication, and clustering.

mechanisms.name: The Incremental Rehash
mechanisms.premise: Redis is single-threaded. A million-entry hash table doubled to two million doesn't need much: allocate the new table, walk the old, copy every entry, free the old. The trouble is that walking a million entries takes order of tens of milliseconds — and during those milliseconds the entire server is unresponsive because the dispatch loop is blocked. For a cache fronting hot user traffic, that is a multi-second p99 tail latency every time the dataset crosses a power-of-two boundary. Most key-value stores accept this cost or move it to a background thread, paying with lock complexity.
mechanisms.candidateRecognition: Every user-facing dict operation does exactly one bucket of rehash work near the top of its body — a single line that amortizes the rehash across thousands of user operations, transforming a tens-of-milliseconds spike into an invisible smear of microseconds per request.

walkthrough.title: The Incremental Rehash
walkthrough.subtitle: Resizing a million-entry hash table takes tens of milliseconds — and Redis is single-threaded. Most databases accept the spike or move it to a background thread. Redis turned the spike into a smear.

opening.problem: Redis is single-threaded. One process, one event loop, one command at a time. The simplicity is the point — there are no locks anywhere in the hot path, no thread-context switches, no synchronization to debug. But it has a price. Any expensive operation done inline blocks every connected client for the duration. A million-entry hash table doubling to two million takes order of tens of milliseconds: allocate a new table, walk the old, copy every entry, free the old. Tens of milliseconds is a multi-second p99 tail every time the keyspace crosses a power-of-two boundary, and for a cache fronting hot user traffic the SLO does not survive that.
opening.tease: Most key-value stores either accept this cost — making rehash one of the documented latency hazards — or move it to a background thread, paying with lock complexity. Redis paid for neither. The rehash still happens; the latency spike does not.
opening.concreteInstance: We follow one specific dict: the global keyspace dict of a Redis instance currently holding 1024 entries, about to grow to 2048. The rehash is triggered at the 1024 → 2048 boundary; rehashidx becomes 0; over the next several thousand user-facing commands, buckets get migrated one per command until ht[0] is empty. A specific DEL command for the key 'session:7c4b3e' arriving mid-rehash sees a transient state we'll trace explicitly: rehashidx = 100, ht[0] has 924 entries left, ht[1] has 100, the key happens to live in ht[1].

scenes.prose:
The naïve operation is the one to keep in mind as the baseline. A dict at load factor > 1 needs to grow. Allocate a new array twice as large; walk every existing entry; rehash its key; place it in the new array; free the old. Single pass, simple code, correct. In a million-entry dict this is roughly a million bucket walks plus a million memcpy's plus a million hash computations — call it 20 milliseconds on a modern CPU. For those 20 milliseconds the single-threaded server processes no commands. Every connected client pauses.

Move the work to a background thread? Now reads have to coordinate with the rehasher: a key might be in the old table, or the new table, or mid-flight between them. The synchronization to handle that — atomic markers, retry loops, hazard pointers — is what Redis explicitly opted out of when it chose single-threading. The whole architectural simplification of Redis collapses if rehashing requires a second thread.

The Redis choice is the third option, the one that doesn't get used much: do the work in tiny pieces, attached to the work the server was already doing. When a dict crosses the load-factor threshold, Redis allocates the new table ht[1] but does not migrate any entries. It sets a flag: `rehashidx = 0`. The dict is now in 'rehashing' state. Every user-facing operation — every dictAdd, dictDelete, dictFind, dictReplace — checks that flag at the top of its body. If set, the operation calls _dictRehashStep, which moves exactly one non-empty bucket from ht[0] to ht[1] and advances rehashidx by 1.

That is the whole scheme. The rehash work that would have taken 20 milliseconds in a single batch is now spread across thousands of user-facing operations, each of which absorbs a few microseconds of rehash work. The total amount of work is unchanged. The distribution is completely different.

embed.question: During the rehash, a DEL for 'session:7c4b3e' arrives. The dict is at rehashidx=100. The key happens to live in ht[1]. What does dictGenericDelete do?
candidates: Looks up only in ht[0], misses, returns 'not found'
Looks up in ht[0] then ht[1], finds it, deletes
Looks up only in ht[1], finds it, deletes
Triggers a full rehash to finish before responding
embed.reveal: During a rehash, every lookup checks BOTH tables. ht[0] has the old positions; ht[1] has the migrated ones. The lookup tries ht[0] first (cheap), and if rehashing it also tries ht[1]. This is the cost the readers pay during the rehash window — slightly slower lookups — and that cost is bounded because the rehash completes after O(N) user operations.

scenes.prose:
The line at the top of every user-facing dict operation that does this work is one conditional call to _dictRehashStep. Look at dictGenericDelete. There is the hash computation, the rehashStep call, then the actual lookup walking ht[0] and (if rehashing) ht[1]. That single line of code — the `if (dictIsRehashing(d)) _dictRehashStep(d)` — is the entire amortization scheme.

Folding that one line into the surrounding lookup logic would obscure why it exists. The line is structurally separate because it carries the architectural invariant: *every user-facing dict operation does exactly one step of rehash work*. The invariant is in one line because Redis is good. Every dict op in the codebase has this one line near the top; spotting it is one of the highest-leverage beacons in the codebase.

The pattern — bound an operation's worst-case latency by amortizing it into other operations the system was already doing — appears across systems code. Garbage collectors do it: incremental mark-sweep does a tiny bit of marking work in every allocation rather than stopping the world. Database compaction does it: leveled compaction in LSM-tree stores chooses a few SSTables to merge per write rather than rewriting everything when a level fills. Window managers do it: the OS's draw-deferred mechanism schedules a small piece of paint work per vblank.

The common shape: an expensive whole-O(N) operation is broken into N tiny pieces of work, each attached to a user-facing operation, so the user pays for the rebalancing they triggered. Redis's incremental rehash is the cleanest small example of the pattern in any open-source codebase.

embed.question: Which of these other Redis subsystems also amortizes a potentially-spiky operation across user-facing calls?
candidates: activeExpireCycle — adapts sweep rate to observed expiration rate
replicationFeedSlaves — buffers writes into a ring backlog
encoding promotion in object.c — silently swaps storage representation
ae.c epoll backend — chooses one of four kernel polling APIs
embed.reveal: activeExpireCycle is the closest cousin: rather than a synchronous scan over all expiring keys (which would block), it samples small random subsets per serverCron call and adapts the iteration budget to the observed hit rate. Different mechanism (sampling vs. work-per-op), same shape (transform a spike into a smear). The other three solve real problems but not this one.

scenes.prose:
The rehash completes when the last non-empty bucket in ht[0] gets migrated; rehashidx returns to -1; the dict drops back to single-table operation; ht[0] is freed. By that point the time-domain spike that *would* have happened — that 20-millisecond block — has been spread across roughly N user-facing operations as a few microseconds per operation each. The total work is the same. The latency profile is unrecognizable.

Nothing in this scheme is sophisticated. There is no clever data structure, no exotic algorithm, no thread machinery. There is one line of code at the top of every dict operation. The cleverness is the *choice* — the architectural decision to pay for rebalancing where the user already was, instead of where the user wasn't.

walkthrough.pullQuote: Every user-facing dict operation does exactly one bucket of rehash work near the top of its body. The architectural invariant is one line of code.

coda.summary: Redis's dict rehash is incremental: every user-facing dictAdd, dictDelete, dictFind calls _dictRehashStep at the top, which moves one bucket from ht[0] to ht[1]. The user pays the cost of growing the table in the operation that triggered the growth, distributed across thousands of subsequent ops. The single-threaded server never blocks for rehashing.

prompts.question: What does _dictRehashStep do in one invocation, and what state does it advance?
Suppose Redis chose to do a full rehash inside dictExpand instead of incrementally. With a 10-million-entry dict, what worst-case p99 latency would clients see during the growth?
In our throughline, the dict was rehashing at rehashidx=100 and the key 'session:7c4b3e' lived in ht[1]. Would the lookup find it on the first table check (ht[0]) or the second (ht[1])?
Name the general pattern: a one-shot O(N) maintenance operation broken into N pieces, each attached to a user-facing call, so per-op latency stays bounded.
What other subsystem in Redis amortizes a spiky operation across multiple invocations? (Hint: the periodic serverCron path.)
If the rehash is incremental and triggered by user ops, what happens if the server suddenly receives no user ops for several minutes after a rehash starts?

mechanisms.name: The Pointer As String
mechanisms.premise: C strings are null-terminated and unsafe; structured-string types like std::string in C++ are safer but their API breaks every C function that expects a char*. Redis needs both: O(1) length, binary safety, amortized-O(1) append — and it needs the strings to be passable straight to printf, sprintf, write(), strcmp() without translation. The two goals seem contradictory.
mechanisms.candidateRecognition: The returned SDS pointer points to the chars, not to the header — the header lives at a negative offset behind the pointer — so an SDS string IS a char* but also has hidden length and capacity available via sdslen() and sdsavail() which read backwards from the pointer.

walkthrough.title: The Pointer As String
walkthrough.subtitle: Custom string types in C usually break every function that takes a char*. Redis wanted the safety of length-prefixed strings AND the compatibility of bare char* — and got both by hiding the header in a place the compiler didn't expect to look.

opening.problem: C strings are null-terminated and unsafe. A binary blob with an embedded zero gets truncated at strcpy; computing a length means walking the whole buffer; appending is O(n) every time. A structured string type — a struct with explicit length + buffer — fixes all of that, but it breaks every C standard-library function that takes a char*. printf, write(2), strcmp, strstr, even the % format specifier — none of them know about your struct. Code calling them gets a pointer to your struct's first field, which is the length, not the chars. The whole point of using C — interop with the world's largest body of code that takes char* — collapses.
opening.tease: Redis's SDS — Simple Dynamic Strings — is structurally a length-prefixed binary-safe type. It is also, at the call site, a plain char*. Both at once. The trick is structural; once you see it, you cannot un-see it.
opening.concreteInstance: We follow one specific SDS string: `s = sdsnew("hello")`. The returned `sds` is, statically, a `typedef char *sds`. Pass it to `printf("%s", s)` and it prints "hello". Pass it to `sdslen(s)` and it returns 5 — without scanning the buffer. The reason both work — and the reason `sdslen` doesn't need a parameter telling it which header struct to read — is what this walkthrough explains.

scenes.prose:
The first thing to look at is the typedef. Line 21 of sds.h declares `typedef char *sds`. That is the type of every SDS string in the codebase. It is, byte-for-byte at the type level, indistinguishable from `char *`. Pass it to a C function and the type checker is satisfied. Cast it back from a `char *` and the type checker is satisfied. There is no struct visible to the call site.

The structs do exist. Just below the typedef, sds.h defines five of them — `sdshdr5`, `sdshdr8`, `sdshdr16`, `sdshdr32`, `sdshdr64` — chosen by string length so a short string carries only 1 byte of header and a giant string can address 64-bit lengths. All five are `__attribute__((__packed__))` so there's no compiler-inserted alignment. Each ends with `char buf[];` — a flexible array member. The header is followed *immediately* in memory by the actual chars.

Now the question — how does an SDS string get *constructed*. `sdsnewlen(init, initlen)` (sds.c:195) is the constructor. It picks the smallest header type that can hold `initlen`, allocates `hdrlen + initlen + 1` bytes (header + chars + NUL terminator), copies the init bytes into the buffer region, sets the header fields. The line that matters most is the return value.

The constructor does **not** return a pointer to the start of the allocation. It returns a pointer to the **buf** field of the header — that is, a pointer to the first char of the actual string data. The header is *before* that pointer in memory. The caller gets back something they can hand to printf. The bookkeeping is hidden at negative offsets.

Look at how `sdslen` reads the length back. The function takes a `const sds s` — a `const char *`, no struct in sight. It needs to know which header type sits behind the pointer. The answer is a one-byte tag stored at `s[-1]` — exactly one byte before the pointer. That byte is the `flags` field of whichever header type is in use; its low 3 bits encode which struct to read.

Switch on those 3 bits. For `SDS_TYPE_8`, cast `s - sizeof(sdshdr8)` back to a `sdshdr8 *`. Read `->len`. Done — O(1), no scan. The header was sitting there the whole time; the trick was that the caller never saw it. The pointer arithmetic walks backwards into memory the *allocator returned but the function signature concealed*.

What this buys is profound. `s` is a `char *`. It works with the entire C standard library. It also has hidden length, hidden capacity (`alloc` field), and hidden type discrimination — all reachable via tiny inline functions that subtract from the pointer and read. The constructor returns a pointer in the middle of an allocation; the destructor takes a pointer in the middle of an allocation and frees the allocation header by subtracting first. Code that wants the safety uses SDS-aware functions; code that wants the compatibility uses the same pointer with C library functions.

There is one rule, and it is the only thing the user must respect: never `free()` an SDS pointer directly. You must call `sdsfree()`, which subtracts to find the allocation start. `free(s)` passes the chars-pointer to the allocator, which doesn't know there's a header behind it, and the free goes wrong. The C language has no way to encode this constraint in the type system; you just have to remember.

embed.question: You write `sds s = sdsnew("hello"); printf("%s, length %zu\n", s, strlen(s));`. What does it print?
embed.reveal: It prints "hello, length 5". printf sees a char* pointing to 'h', 'e', 'l', 'l', 'o', '\0' and stops at the null. strlen scans the same chars and returns 5. The SDS header is sitting at s[-something] but no C-library function reaches there. Everything works as if you had written `char s[] = "hello"` — *plus* sdslen(s) is O(1) and you have a free-buffer field for amortized appends.

scenes.prose:
The same idea recurs once you know to look for it. Object headers in JavaScript V8 are hidden at negative offsets from the value pointer. Reference counts in many C++ shared_ptr implementations live at -16 bytes from the controlled object pointer when the control block is fused with the object. Malloc-aware free implementations look at the bytes just before the user pointer to find the chunk header. The general shape: the type system shows the user a `T*`, but the implementation puts metadata *before* the T in memory, accessible only to code that knows about it. The user pointer is a viewport into a larger structure; the structure's other fields are reachable by subtracting.

SDS is the cleanest small example of the pattern in any open-source C codebase. Five header variants, one flags byte at s[-1], one tiny switch statement in every accessor. The reader of SDS code that does not know this trick will spend an afternoon being confused by the inline functions. The reader who knows it sees them immediately.

walkthrough.pullQuote: The constructor returns a pointer not to the start of the allocation but to its char buffer — the header sits at negative offsets, invisible to every C library function but reachable by everyone who knows it's there.

coda.summary: Redis's SDS strings are typedef'd as plain char*. The structural data — length, capacity, type discriminator — lives in a header packed immediately before the chars in memory. Every SDS accessor subtracts from the pointer to find the header; every consumer of the chars passes the pointer directly to printf, strcmp, write, etc. and gets correct behavior. One pointer, two memory regions, one type to the type checker.

prompts.question: In an SDS string of type SDS_TYPE_8, where exactly does the length field sit relative to the returned sds pointer? Express your answer in bytes.
What would happen if a user wrote `free(s)` instead of `sdsfree(s)` on an SDS string of type SDS_TYPE_16?
Why is the sds typedef `char *` and not `void *` or a struct? What does the choice buy and what does it cost?
For `s = sdsnew("hello")`, what is at memory address s[-1]?

Name the general pattern: a constructor returns a pointer not to the start of its allocation but to a field inside it, with metadata at known negative offsets only the accessor functions know to read.
Where else in Redis (or in any C codebase you know) does a pointer's metadata live at a fixed negative offset from the pointer itself?

mechanisms.name: The OS As Snapshot
mechanisms.premise: Snapshotting a running in-memory database is two problems: get a consistent point-in-time view of memory, and write it to disk without blocking the foreground server. The conventional approach is a long-running write transaction or a copy-on-write data structure with software bookkeeping. Either solution requires deep cooperation from every data type in the database; both add cycles to the hot path; both grow more fragile as the data model grows. Redis solved both problems by writing zero such code.
mechanisms.candidateRecognition: rdbSaveBackground forks the process; the OS's copy-on-write fork() semantics give the child a consistent memory snapshot for free, and the parent keeps serving traffic while the kernel CoWs only the pages the parent modifies during the save.

walkthrough.title: The OS As Snapshot
walkthrough.subtitle: Snapshotting a live in-memory database is two problems: get a consistent point-in-time view, and write it without blocking. Most databases solve both by writing thousands of lines of cooperation code. Redis solved both by writing zero.

opening.problem: An in-memory database that survives a crash needs to occasionally write its full state to disk. The single-threaded server process holds gigabytes of live data in memory — keyspace dicts, value strings, list and hash structures — and it is constantly mutating that data as new commands arrive. Snapshotting that state is two problems running into each other: getting a consistent point-in-time view despite ongoing mutations, and writing gigabytes of bytes to disk slowly without blocking the server's command loop. Conventional solutions require deep cooperation from every data type — long-running write transactions, copy-on-write data structures, software-emulated multiversioning. Each one adds bytes to every hot-path operation and cycles to every read.
opening.tease: Redis writes zero such code. It does not maintain transactions; it does not version its data structures; it does not even know what "snapshot consistency" means. And yet `BGSAVE` produces a consistent point-in-time snapshot of the entire keyspace while the server continues serving traffic at full speed.
opening.concreteInstance: We follow one specific BGSAVE. A Redis instance is holding 4 GB of live data; 200 connected clients are issuing roughly 10,000 commands per second; the user types `BGSAVE` at the redis-cli. Forty-five seconds later, an RDB file on disk contains a byte-for-byte consistent snapshot of the dataset as it existed at the moment BGSAVE was invoked. During those 45 seconds, the server's p99 command latency stays under a millisecond. The clients never noticed.

scenes.prose:
The function that starts a background save is `rdbSaveBackground` in `rdb.c`. By any reasonable software-engineering standard it is shockingly short. It validates that no other child process is currently running. It records some stats. Then it calls `redisFork(CHILD_TYPE_RDB)` and branches on the return value.

`fork()` is a 1970s-vintage Unix system call. It creates a new process whose memory is, immediately after the call, identical to the parent's memory. Two processes, two PIDs, same data. In the parent, fork returns the child's PID. In the child, fork returns 0. That is the entirety of the call's contract.

The child branch is where the snapshot work happens. The child calls `rdbSave(filename, ...)`, which walks the in-memory keyspace dict, encodes every key-value pair into the RDB binary format, and writes it to the named file. The child then exits.

During those 45 seconds the child is walking the dataset, what is the parent doing? It is continuing to serve traffic. Clients are sending GET, SET, DEL, LPUSH, ZADD; the parent is mutating the keyspace; commands are landing at 10,000 per second. The parent never blocks. The parent does not coordinate with the child. The parent does not read a snapshot marker, take a lock, version a key, or notify anyone. The parent runs exactly as if `rdbSaveBackground` had returned immediately to its single user — because in the parent's memory space, it did.

Here is what makes this work, and it is a property of the operating system, not of Redis. When fork() returns, the parent and child *appear* to have separate copies of memory, but they don't — they share the same physical pages, marked read-only. As long as both processes only *read*, no copy is made. The instant the parent writes to a page — a single byte mutation anywhere in those 4 GB — the kernel transparently allocates a fresh physical page, copies the original page contents to it, points the parent's virtual address at the new page, and lets the write proceed. The child still sees the original page. The child still sees what was there at the moment of fork.

This is copy-on-write, and it is the mechanism the entire Redis snapshot architecture rests on. The fork() call gave the child a logically-consistent view of every byte the parent owned at the instant of forking. The OS's virtual memory subsystem maintains that consistency without Redis writing a line of code to enforce it. The parent's mutations, after the fork, cost one extra page-copy each, paid by the kernel, invisible to either process.

embed.question: During the 45-second BGSAVE, a client sends `SET counter 42`. The 'counter' key was already in memory at the time of the fork with value '17'. What does the child write to the RDB file for the 'counter' key?
candidates: 17 — the value at the time of the fork
An error indicating the data changed mid-snapshot
embed.reveal: The child writes 17 — the value at the time of the fork. The parent's SET modified its own copy of the page (CoW'd by the kernel); the child still sees the original page containing 17. The RDB snapshot is point-in-time consistent: it captures the state exactly at the instant rdbSaveBackground was called, regardless of what the parent does next.

scenes.prose:
The cost analysis is worth a moment. The child process inherits all 4 GB of the parent's virtual memory, but no physical pages are copied at fork time — they are shared and marked read-only. The kernel needs only a few milliseconds to set up the page table mappings. So the fork itself is cheap.

During the snapshot, the parent's mutations trigger CoW page copies. The cost is proportional to the *write rate* during the save, not to the *dataset size*. A heavily-written database during a 45-second save might CoW a meaningful fraction of its pages and effectively double its memory usage transiently. A read-mostly database snapshots almost for free. The architectural tradeoff is honest: Redis is optimized for read-heavy and burst-write workloads precisely because that is where this scheme produces the best results.

The same fork+CoW trick appears unchanged in `rewriteAppendOnlyFileBackground` (aof.c) — AOF rewrite forks, child writes a compacted log, parent buffers new commands and ships them to the child at the end. And in `replicationFeedSlaves` indirectly: a new replica syncs by triggering a fork-based RDB transfer. Every persistence-adjacent operation in Redis routes through fork.

What this codebase did not have to write to make BGSAVE work: a multiversion concurrency control system; a snapshot transaction protocol; a write-ahead log; cooperative copy-on-write data structures; locks on the keyspace; a background snapshot thread with its own scheduling. What it did write: a fork call and a few status checks. The actual snapshot machinery — point-in-time consistency, isolation from concurrent writes, the entire algorithm — is a feature of Unix that has been present since the 1970s and that Redis simply asks for by name.

For a piece of software whose performance is the entire reason it exists, the most striking design choice is sometimes the absence of an algorithm. The OS is doing the work.

walkthrough.pullQuote: Redis does not snapshot its memory. It forks, and the kernel's copy-on-write semantics produce the snapshot for free — point-in-time consistent, isolated from concurrent writes, with no cooperation from any data structure inside the database.

coda.summary: Redis's BGSAVE is twenty lines of C around a single fork() call. The child inherits a copy-on-write view of the parent's entire memory; the OS lazily copies any page the parent subsequently mutates. The child walks the dataset and writes it to disk in the consistent state it had at fork time; the parent continues serving traffic uninterrupted. The same trick powers AOF rewrite and replication's initial sync. Redis writes no snapshot-isolation code; it asks the operating system to provide the isolation, which the kernel has been able to do since the 1970s.

prompts.question: After `rdbSaveBackground` calls `redisFork(CHILD_TYPE_RDB)`, what is the return value in the parent process versus the child process?
Suppose the parent has a 4 GB dataset and writes to every page during a 45-second BGSAVE. How much extra memory does the system use at the peak?
Approximately how long does the fork() call itself take, and what is the dominant cost during the rest of the BGSAVE window?
In the worked example, a client SETs `counter` from 17 to 42 during the BGSAVE. What does the RDB file contain for that key, and why?
Name the general design pattern: an in-process algorithm is replaced by asking the operating system to provide the equivalent semantics via a single system call.
Where else in Redis is fork() used for the same purpose? Cite at least one other file/function.

mechanisms.name: The Encoding Promotion
mechanisms.premise: Most real Redis workloads contain millions of small data structures — hashes with 3 keys, sorted sets with 12 members, lists of 4 elements. Each of those, naïvely, would carry the overhead of a real hash table or skip list — hundreds of bytes of pointers per data structure. With a million small hashes the overhead alone exceeds the data. But the same code paths must also serve a hash with 10 million entries, where the real hash table is the only viable representation.
mechanisms.candidateRecognition: Every Redis object carries an encoding tag pointing to the cheapest representation that currently fits — listpack for small, hashtable for large — and the type implementation in t_hash.c (and t_zset.c, t_list.c, …) silently promotes from one to the other when a size threshold is crossed, so a hash that grew from 3 entries to 300 silently swapped storage strategies under your fingers.

mechanisms.name: The Resumable Stream
mechanisms.premise: A Redis replica syncing with its master needs the whole dataset on first sync (an expensive operation involving fork() + RDB streaming) and then a continuous stream of every write command. A flaky network drops the connection every few minutes. Resyncing the whole dataset every time the connection blinks is unacceptable — the master would constantly be forking. The naïve solution is connection-level retry, but TCP can't recover after a disconnect.
mechanisms.candidateRecognition: Every replication command is tagged with a monotonic master_repl_offset; the master keeps a bounded in-memory backlog ring buffer; a reconnecting replica asks for everything since offset N, and if N is still inside the backlog the master ships a delta instead of a full RDB.

mechanisms.name: The Adaptive Sweeper
mechanisms.premise: Redis keys can have TTLs; expired keys need to be deleted. Lazy expiration (check on read) is cheap but leaks memory if many expired keys are never read. Eager expiration (background scan) is correct but costs CPU whether or not the rate of expirations is high. A static scan rate is wrong both ways.
mechanisms.candidateRecognition: activeExpireCycle samples a small random subset per call and adapts its iteration budget to the observed hit rate — under heavy expiration load it sweeps more aggressively; under light load it backs off — so the work scales with the actual rate of expiration, not with the size of the keyspace.

mechanisms.name: The Platform Seam
mechanisms.premise: Redis must run on Linux (epoll), BSDs and macOS (kqueue), Solaris (evport), and as a fallback on any POSIX system (select). Each kernel API is different. Most cross-platform code wraps this difference in #ifdefs scattered through the codebase, eroding readability and turning every platform issue into a forensic exercise.
mechanisms.candidateRecognition: ae.c declares a tiny six-function event-API surface (aeApiCreate, aeApiAddEvent, aeApiDelEvent, aeApiPoll, aeApiResize, aeApiName); each backend lives in exactly one file (ae_epoll.c, ae_kqueue.c, ae_evport.c, ae_select.c); a single #include at the top of ae.c chooses the right one at compile time — so the rest of the event loop reads as if there were no platforms.
